I might have missed reply about the screen.
the unit is now having issues with the auo-fan settings.

Its auto fan isn't regulating to temperature. It held about 80–82% at 45°C and at 56°C, and dropped right back there after every restart.

not sure if it's a fault or just how this firmware's auto mode is built: a fixed, aggressive fan level rather than a temperature curve. The readings look the same either way.

auto fan at 80–82% with the chip at 45–56°C.

i set manual fan speed at 40% manual, the chip still holds 55–57°C.

overall, not the best experience with this thing.

you were right, it doesn’t make the OG 120 MH/s rate but it does beat the advertised 105

still not sure how to feel about getting a unit swapped without my approval, but y’all have been so nice, i just accepted it.

any insight as to a fan issue would be helpful. it’s too darn loud at 80% all day and all night.

(it’s 4am in Hawaii and i’ve been working on this for an hour trying to get it to be quieter)

thanks for the help.

-kyle

Sent from my iPhone

Hi Kyle,

Good news on the fan: what you are seeing is not a fault. You diagnosed it correctly yourself. The stock DC02 auto mode is not a temperature curve, it is a fixed, deliberately aggressive level, so it sits around 80 percent whether the chip is at 45 or at 56 degrees, and it returns to that level on every restart. Three things confirm the hardware is healthy: the fan responds instantly when you set it manually, 40 percent holds the chip at 55 to 57 degrees, and you are hashing above the advertised rate. A unit with a cooling or sensor problem would climb and throttle, not sit flat.

So for the noise, stay in manual. 40 percent at 55 to 57 degrees is a comfortable place for a scrypt chip of this generation, it is nowhere near the throttle point, and you can run it there around the clock. If you want a little margin for a hot afternoon in Hawaii, 50 percent is the usual sweet spot. I would not go below about 30 percent, and after any change give it 30 minutes and check the temperature once before you go to bed. Keep the intake side clear of the desk or a wall, since on this chassis airflow does more than fan percentage does.

One thing worth knowing: if the manual setting drops back to auto after a power cycle, save it, leave the unit running a minute or two so the setting is written, and then power cycle. If it still reverts, tell me and I will dig into that specifically, because the setting is meant to persist.

The real cure for the noise is Harlo OS, our own firmware, free, and the Hammer DC02 is on its supported list. It gives you an actual auto fan curve instead of one fixed level, plus quad pools, Stratum V2 and wall measured power. You flash it from your browser: open harlolabs.com in Chrome or Edge, pick the DC02 profile, connect the miner with a USB data cable, erase and install, about two minutes. The first install uses the factory image, which erases your saved wifi and pool settings, so have your pool URL and worker name handy to type back in. After that, updates are over the air and keep your settings.

One safety note while you are in firmware land: do not flash Hammer's own DC02-APP 2.x.x image onto a 1.x.x unit, as Hammer warns that this damages the device. Harlo OS picks the right image for you, which is another reason I would go that route.

And yes, you were right about the hashrate too. The H. tune does not reach the old 120, but beating the 105 it is rated for means your unit is running well.

If you want to compare fan curves with other DC02 owners or ping our hardware lead directly, the Discord is at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf and JD is @nullhashrate there. He is very active and it is the fastest route at 4am Hawaii time. Otherwise just reply here and I will stay with you until it is quiet.

Thanks for your patience through all of this, Kyle.

Hal, HeliumDeploy Technical Support
